youtube_description:
The duel at Funashima is usually told as a late arrival, a carved oar and a single blow. That version comes from the winner's side: a stone raised by Musashi's adopted son, and biographies written by his school more than a century later. Another record, kept by the family that held Moji Castle on the strait, tells it differently, and does not agree on how Sasaki Kojiro died. If you stood on that castle wall, which record would you trust: the stone's, or the castle's?

📰 Your reporter: Tokio Kamiya, a former Tokyo foreign correspondent. His grandfather's brass pocket watch carries him to one day of Japan's past at a time. He can watch and he can speak, but he can never change what happens. This time he files his dispatch from Moji Castle in 1612, on the day a later biography gives for the duel across the strait.

scenes.narration: The island is called Funashima, Ship Island. From the wall I see a low dark shape in the haze, in the strait between the Kyushu shore, where Kokura lies, and the main island of Honshu. One day it will carry another name, Ganryujima, after the loser, whom the oldest record calls only Ganryu. Nothing is built on it. Nobody lives there. I have a problem, and I want to say it plainly: everything I know about today comes from people who were not here, writing at very different times.

scenes.narration: I open my notebook to the oldest record. It is a stone monument, carved in 1654 in Kokura, forty-two years from now. Miyamoto Iori raised it, as Musashi's adopted son. It says the two men met at the same moment, that Musashi struck with a wooden blade, and that the man it names only as Ganryu fell. No late arrival. No carved oar. No shouting across the water. I note who paid for the stone, and I note what it leaves out.

scenes.narration: The second record is younger, from around 1672. It was kept in the Numata family, the family of this castle's warden. I think it matters who they were. They were not Musashi's heirs, and they were not Kojiro's. They served the Hosokawa, and in their own telling this castle has a part in the day. That gives them no reason to flatter Musashi, and every reason to remember their own part. I weigh both. And their story does not start on the island. It starts in Kokura, with an argument between students.

scenes.narration: A sentry on the wall sees my notebook and takes me for a travelling merchant. I let him. He says the talk in Kokura town is of two fencing teachers who meet on that island today. He grins and asks which one I would bet on. I tell him I never bet on what I cannot see. He shrugs and points at the island. I note that he is repeating talk, not news. The Numata record gives the reason he does not: the teachers' students had argued over whose master was stronger, until the masters had to settle it.

scenes.narration: Now a problem with the loser himself. The oldest record gives only the name Ganryu. The Numata record calls him Kojiro, with no family name. The surname Sasaki first joins Kojiro in a biography of 1776, and some scholars wonder whether it came from a stage play of 1737. As for age, that same biography says eighteen. It also names his teacher as a master of the mid-1500s, which, some argue, would make him an old man, perhaps near seventy. So the beautiful young genius may be a later picture. I mark both readings. I do not choose.

scenes.narration: Here is a silence I find hard to ignore. Near the end of his life Musashi wrote the Book of Five Rings, in 1645. In it he says he won more than sixty contests and never lost. As far as I can find, it names neither Ganryu nor this island. He left no account of the most famous fight of his life. The people who did write it were his adopted son, and later the schools that carried his name. I read no motive into that. I only note where the story's first pages came from.

None of it is in the stone of 1654, and none of it is in the Numata record. It appears in the biographies written by Musashi's own school, the fullest in 1776, about 160 years after today. I am not saying it is false. I am saying nobody here wrote it down. I close the notebook, because behind me something is happening at the gate.

scenes.narration: So here is what the Numata record says happened out on the island, and I repeat it only as its claim. The two men had agreed to fight one against one. Kojiro came alone, as agreed. Several of Musashi's students crossed in secret. Musashi struck Kojiro down, and then, says the record, Kojiro drew breath again, and those students beat him to death. The stone and the later biographies have none of this; for them it ends with one blow. I did not see it. The wall did not see it either. Weigh it for yourself.

scenes.narration: The record goes on. Kojiro's students go after Musashi, and he runs into this castle. Nobumoto shelters him, then sends him under an armed escort to his father in Bungo. If it is true, the man who won Japan's most famous duel spent the hours after it behind this gate, in someone else's care. I look at the gate now. It is shut. A guard leans against it. I cannot see inside, and I cannot tell you what happened behind it. I can tell you the Numata family had every reason to remember it, and every reason to be proud of it.

scenes.narration: Let me weigh the stone. Iori owed his father honour, and a monument is not a courtroom. It is carved to praise. A flight to a castle gate is not what a family chooses to cut into stone. I do not say the stone lies. I say it was made to honour one man, and what honours him is what it keeps. The Numata record has its own purpose, a family wanting its castle in the story. Neither writer was here. Neither can be asked. Each kept what served the people they wrote for.

scenes.narration: So the island is named for the loser, and the story for the winner. In time sailors will call the little island Ganryu, and travellers will cross to stand where he fell. I walk down from the wall with that thought, and I do not know who got the better part.

scenes.narration: Reporter's note. Back in my own century, I try to say how a record becomes the standard story. A stone is carved, and stones last. A school copies its master's biography, and copies survive. A stage play in 1737 may have lent the loser a surname, and a novelist in 1935 gave him a face. I think Kojiro remains the genius who lost in a single stroke because the records from the winner's side were the ones kept, copied and retold until they became the standard.

scenes.narration: Reporter's note. I should be fair to the winner's side. A later biography is not worthless because it came late; it may hold memories that no stone could carry. scenes.narration: Reporter's note. I think the lesson here is not about Kojiro alone. In any dispute, the story that gets carved, printed and taught is the story of the people who could afford to carve, print and teach it. Kojiro left no writing in any record I carry.
